The waterflea Eurycercus lamellatus, a common littoral cladoceran of northern temperate lakes, exhibits a well-documented suite of life-history traits shaped by thermal conditions. In laboratory cultures maintained at a constant 12 °C [T = 12 °C], freshly released neonates measure approximately 0.074 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.074 centimeters] from the anterior margin of the head to the posterior rim of the carapace. This diminutive birth length reflects the limited scope for maternal provisioning within the parthenogenetic brood chamber and is typical of the genus. The timing of release is also tightly constrained by temperature, with the age at birth being about 5 days [ab = about 5 days] under these same incubation conditions, a value that aligns well with developmental rate estimates for other chydorid cladocerans at comparable thermal regimes at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. Such rapid early life-cycle progression is ecologically advantageous, permitting multiple generations within a single growing season in ephemeral or resource-variable habitats.

As juveniles progress through successive instars, they undergo substantial somatic growth culminating in the attainment of an ultimate body length that differs markedly between the sexes. Females, which represent the overwhelmingly dominant morph under parthenogenetic reproduction, reach a maximum total length of 0.40 centimeters [Li = 0.40 centimeters], a size that places Eurycercus lamellatus among the larger members of the Chydoridae. This ultimate length is achieved after several moults and is accompanied by the development of a robust, heavily sclerotized carapace. Males, which arise only in response to environmental cues promoting sexual reproduction, are considerably more diminutive. Their growth trajectory plateaus at a far smaller dimension, with an ultimate total length for males of just 0.14 centimeters [Li = 0.14 centimeters], a pronounced sexual size dimorphism that reflects divergent life-history priorities between the obligately parthenogenetic females and the short-lived, gamete-producing males.

The onset of reproductive competence in Eurycercus lamellatus is marked by a distinct size threshold rather than a rigid chronological age, a pattern common among cladocerans where growth is moult-dependent. Puberty, defined as the instar at which the first clutch of parthenogenetic eggs is deposited into the brood chamber, occurs when an individual achieves a total length at puberty of approximately 0.18 centimeters [Lp = approximately 0.18 centimeters]. Reaching this threshold requires the successful completion of several pre-reproductive moults and is contingent upon adequate food availability in the form of epiphytic algae and detritus. Field-collected specimens often attain this size by the late juvenile or early sub-adult phase, and the transition is accompanied by a detectable shift in the allometric scaling of the carapace. This body-length criterion for maturity is evolutionarily conserved within the family and is energetically linked to the capacity to accommodate a fully developed clutch of eggs within the limited space of the dorsal brood pouch.

Reproductive output in the waterflea is a function of both clutch size and the rapidity of the moulting cycle, both of which are strongly temperature-dependent. At the standard experimental temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females carrying a full complement of subitaneous eggs produce an average of 10 eggs per brood [N_R_i = 10 eggs per brood], reflecting the high fecundity potential of the species. The inter-brood interval, or the duration between successive moults, averages 9 days per moult [F_R_i = 9 days per moult], a period that includes egg development within the brood chamber and the subsequent release of neonates before the next exuviation. The resultant daily reproductive rate, derived from these two parameters, thus stands at a maximum of 10/9 offspring per female per day, a formulation that highlights the continuous, overlapping generations produced during the parthenogenetic phase. This productivity is critical for population persistence in littoral zones subject to variable predation pressure from fish and invertebrates.

Comparative physiological studies reveal that the life-history schedule of Eurycercus lamellatus is finely attuned to its cool-temperate habitat. The age at birth of about 5 days [ab = about 5 days] recorded at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] lengthens considerably at lower temperatures, such as the 11.75-day developmental period observed at 10 °C, while it shortens to 5.97 days at 15 °C, demonstrating a nonlinear thermal response typical of crustacean embryogenesis. Similarly, the number of eggs per brood, also measured under the same 12 °C [T = 12 °C] conditions, reaches up to 10 eggs per brood [N_R_i = up to 10 eggs per brood], with the 9-day moulting interval [F_R_i = the 9-day moulting interval] serving as a baseline for calculating population growth rates. The ultimate female length of 0.40 centimeters [Li = 0.40 centimeters] provides a substantial body volume for egg carriage, contrasting sharply with the male ultimate length of 0.14 centimeters [Li = 0.14 centimeters], which limits males to a purely gametic role. Overall, the species' strategy of early maturation at approximately 0.18 centimeters [Lp = approximately 0.18 centimeters] and high iteroparity under favorable thermal regimes underscores its success as a dominant grazer in shallow, vegetated lake margins.
